summary: This memo gives naming guidelines for X.500 directory pilots, meaning the early experimental directory services run by different countries and organisations. It recommends how entries should be named so the separate pilots fit together into one coherent global directory. It is informational. It was replaced by RFC 1617.

plainLanguage.summary: When lots of people build phone books, they should agree on how names are written so every book can be combined into one big book. This paper suggests those naming rules.

questions: how to name entries in an x500 directory
how deep should a directory tree be
should organizations use acronyms in directory names
how to name multinational organizations in x500
subtitle: How directory pilot projects should name entries to fit together globally

tldr.problem: As multiple organizations built experimental X.500 directory services, they used inconsistent naming conventions, making it hard to link the separate directories into one global system.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends a shared structure with guidelines for naming countries, organizations, organizational units, and people, emphasizing flat trees, full names over acronyms, and consistent formats across pilots.
tldr.outcome: These guidelines helped early directory pilots interoperate and provided a foundation for centralized X.500 deployments, though the technology was eventually superseded by DNS and LDAP.

today: RFC 1384 is an Informational document that was obsoleted by RFC 1617 in 1994. It reflected best practices for X.500 directory pilots of its era, but the directory technology it describes was eventually superseded by DNS for general Internet use and later by LDAP for directory services.

sections.title: Introduction and DIT Structure
sections.content:
RFC 1384 provides naming guidelines for X.500 directory pilots, the experimental directory services being deployed by different countries and organizations in the early 1990s. The core problem is establishing a consistent structure for the Directory Information Tree (DIT)—the hierarchy that holds entries for countries, organizations, people, and services.

The top level of the DIT holds country entries, which serve as anchors for organization entries within that country. At the root level, there are also entries for international organizations (such as the Internet itself) and a few localities (such as Europe or Africa) to serve as parent nodes for supra-national organizations. This structure allows the separate pilots to be combined into one coherent global directory.
sections.plainLanguage: The directory is like a tree. Countries are at the bottom of the tree, companies are on the branches, and people are at the ends. Everyone agrees on this shape so the trees can be connected.

sections.title: Naming Style and Organization Names
sections.content:
The RFC advocates for full, recognizable names in the directory rather than acronyms or abbreviations. For organizations, the RDN (Relative Distinguished Name) should use the organization's full name—University College London rather than UCL, for example. The argument is twofold: full names are more meaningful to users, and they are less likely to be challenged in a registration process (UCL could mean United Carriers Ltd). Acronyms and abbreviations should be stored as alternative values of the naming attribute so that searches can find them.

The same principle applies to organizational units within companies. A department abbreviated as CS in common parlance might mean Computer Science, Computing Services, Cognitive Science, or Clinical Science. Using the full name in the RDN and storing abbreviations as alternatives supports both browsing and searching.

For people, a consistent naming format is recommended—typically a familiar first name followed by the surname, such as Steve Hardcastle-Kille, with alternative names stored separately. This approach helps user interfaces rank matches appropriately and allows users to search by the name they know.
sections.plainLanguage: Write out whole names, not just initials. 'Computer Science' instead of 'CS'. If you know a nickname, write that down too so people can find it when they search.

sections.title: Tree Depth and Structure
sections.content:
A key recommendation is that the DIT should be as flat as possible. Long directory names with many levels are harder to remember, less intuitive, and harder for users to navigate. The RFC suggests that most DIT depth comes from two sources: first, how many levels of countries and organizations are present at the top (determined by registration authorities), and second, whether large organizations sub-divide themselves with multiple levels of organizational units.

For the second factor, the RFC recommends a maximum of two levels of organizational units, even for large organizations. Organizations with only dozens or hundreds of employees should not use organizational units at all. When unique naming is difficult (for instance, multiple people with the same name), the RFC suggests using multi-valued RDNs that combine a common name with other attributes like a title or organizational unit to disambiguate.
sections.plainLanguage: Don't make the directory too deep or complicated. Two or three levels of sub-organization is usually enough. This keeps the paths short and easy to remember.

sections.title: Naming Multi-National Organizations
sections.content:
The RFC examines how to represent multi-national organizations in the directory. The X.500 standard says that only international organizations may be placed at the root; multi-national organizations must be represented as separate entries underneath their respective country entries. The RFC discusses three approaches for structuring these entries in the DIT.

The single-entity model treats the multi-national as one organization under one country, using aliases to point to entries in other countries. This is suitable for highly centralized organizations. The loose-confederation model represents the organization separately under each country where it operates, with aliases or seeAlso links to bind the parts together. The loosely-linked model avoids aliases entirely and relies on attributes like seeAlso to indicate relationships, allowing each part to be essentially independent.

Each approach has trade-offs in terms of naming naturalness, organization-wide search capability, and flexibility in representing different views of the structure. The RFC recommends selecting the model that best fits the actual governance structure of the organization.
sections.plainLanguage: A big company with offices in many countries can be shown in the directory in different ways: as one big company with branches, as separate companies linked together, or just as separate companies that mention each other.

sections.title: Miscellaneous Guidelines
sections.content:
The RFC covers two additional topics that frequently arise in directory implementation. First, alias schema consistency ensures that aliases are set up correctly: the RDN of the alias should be a valid name for the entry it points to, and if the aliased object were placed where the alias is, it should violate no schema rules.

Second, the RFC notes that some organizations can be either independent organizations or organizational units of a parent, depending on their location in the DIT. To support this, an entry should be allowed to have both the organization and organizationalUnit object classes, enabling an organization to exist as both an independent entity and a sub-unit of a larger entity in different parts of the tree.
sections.plainLanguage: When you create a shortcut in the directory (an alias), make sure it points to the right kind of entry. And let organizations be departments too, in different parts of the tree.
